sections.text: Same eggs. Same store. Same time. Five different prices. This isn't a glitch. Researchers sent four hundred thirty-seven real shoppers to buy the exact same groceries at the exact same moment, and three out of four items showed up at more than one price. Welcome to the new pricing game. Companies are testing what you will pay, not what the product is worth. Today: how it works, what changed in twenty twenty-six, and five ways to protect your wallet.

In December twenty twenty-five, Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union ran a study on Instacart. They had four hundred thirty-seven shoppers in four cities fill identical carts at the same store, during coordinated time windows. About three out of four items showed up at more than one price. Some shoppers paid up to twenty-three percent more for the same item. Cart totals varied about seven percent on average. The researchers estimated that could cost a family of four about twelve hundred dollars a year. A box of saltines at a Target in Ohio: three ninety-nine for some people, four sixty-nine for others. To be fair: Instacart said these were random price tests, not based on personal or demographic data, and the study didn't find a clear link to demographics. But after the report, Instacart ended all item price tests on its platform, and both the FTC and New York's attorney general started asking questions. So here's the real question: if prices can already change from person to person, what happens when they're set using your data?

That's what regulators now call surveillance pricing: using personal data to guess the highest price you, specifically, are willing to pay. In January twenty twenty-five, the FTC published early findings from a study of companies that build pricing tools for retailers, including Mastercard, Accenture, McKinsey and others. Staff found these tools can use your location, your browsing and purchase history, your mouse movements on a page, and even what you leave in your cart without buying. Think about what that means. Hesitating over the buy button is data. Coming back three times to the same product is data. Shopping from an expensive phone? Data. One important point: the FTC's findings were preliminary, and the examples it shared were hypothetical, because the company data is confidential. It's not proof that every store does this. It shows the tools exist, and they're being sold.

Here's what's new. In twenty twenty-six, states stopped just studying this, and started banning it. Maryland went first. Since October first, twenty twenty-six, large grocery stores and grocery delivery apps can't use personal data to set individual prices, and in-store prices must hold for at least one business day. The catch: consumer groups point to loopholes, like loyalty program pricing. Connecticut followed, with a law signed this year that bans surveillance pricing by retail sellers and food delivery services, and requires an online label when personal data is used to raise a price.

Then New Jersey. On July twenty-third, twenty twenty-six, it banned grocery stores and delivery apps from varying prices based on personal data. It's the first state where shoppers themselves can sue, with penalties up to fifty thousand dollars per violation. Stores have until August first, twenty twenty-seven to comply. New York took a different path. It doesn't ban the practice, but since November twenty twenty-five, companies must show this exact sentence: This price was set by an algorithm using your personal data. And it's spreading. Over forty bills in more than twenty-four states were pending this summer. At the federal level, in August twenty twenty-six, the FTC proposed a policy saying hidden personalized pricing can be deceptive or unfair. It's a proposal, not a ban. The FTC itself says Congress hasn't given it the power to outlaw the practice everywhere.

Notice those small digital price tags showing up in stores? They let a store change prices across an entire aisle in seconds. That isn't automatically bad. Stores say it saves labor. But it's why Maryland now requires grocery prices to hold for at least a business day, and why New Jersey paused new installations. Lawmakers are worried prices could change during the day, depending on who's in the store, and when.

You can't turn this off completely. But you can make it much harder to target you. One. Compare before you buy. Check the same item logged out, in a private window, or on another device, or ask someone else to check it. If the price changes, you just learned something. Two. Watch the cart game. If prices drop after you leave something in your cart, that's your data at work. Be careful with that trick, because prices can go up too. Three. Know what your loyalty card really costs. The discounts are real, but they're a data trade. And in Maryland, loyalty program pricing is one of the loopholes. Four. Look for the label. In New York, if you see this price was set by an algorithm using your personal data, you're looking at personalized pricing. Shop around. Five. Report it. If you live in a state with a ban, report suspected violations to your state attorney general. And in New Jersey, starting in twenty twenty-seven, shoppers can sue.

For decades, the price tag was the same for everyone in the store. That's quietly changing. WorthWired decodes the American money system, so it stops decoding you. Subscribe, and send this to the person who does your family's grocery shopping.
